thread.title: Do bad earnings herald an economic slowdown? - MarketWatch

author: Tim Mullaney
title: Do bad earnings herald an economic slowdown? - MarketWatch
text:
On the face of it, Tuesday’s earnings report from Dow Jones Industrial Average member 3M wasn’t so bad: Third-quarter profit per share rose 11%, while revenue in dollars slipped a bit, led by currency fluctuations and a slowdown in sales to China.
Then 3M shares MMM, -3.07% dropped 8%. Mr. Market was not amused. 3M’s woes took the Dow DJIA, -0.97% with them for a spell, as the index fell 500 points before recovering most losses before the bell. (3M regained almost half of its loss).
Earnings from United Technologies UTX, -3.81% , which beat forecasts modestly, a warning from Texas Instruments TXN, -4.61% , and a big miss from Caterpillar CAT, -3.32% , which cited rising costs partly related to President Donald Trump’s tariffs on aluminum, didn’t help the mood.
See Also Interest in Midterms Has Surged Among These Demographic Groups × So what does this mean? Does it mean a recession soon, or at least an end to the long bull market that will, Trump’s bluster notwithstanding, forever be ascribed to his predecessor’s skillful intervention after 2008’s financial crisis?
“I think profit growth has topped out and will definitively slow going forward, contributing to the next recession, likely early in the next decade,” said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “Historically, profit growth peaks approximately two years prior to downturns.”
But first, let’s put the earnings misses so far into perspective, with some help from Bank of America Merrill Lynch.
Through Friday, earnings reports from 85 companies in the Standard & Poor’s 500 SPX, -1.23% stock index had been released — and consensus quarterly earnings for the quarter had risen slightly after those results, as analysts factored in better-than-expected results from banks such as Goldman Sachs GS, -2.03% and JPMorgan Chase JPM, -1.07% , as well as video-streaming service Netflix NFLX, -3.83% .
But for the first time since 2000, the market isn’t rewarding companies that beat on earnings — and companies that beat on sales are actually underperforming slightly. Those are late-bull-market signals, Merrill strategist Savita Subramanian writes.
This week is the key, since so many companies are set to report, with most of the rest set to report by Nov. 2. (That’s before the election, not that most voters will be very attuned to earnings, or putting much stock in market movements unless they are unexpectedly big in either direction).
Merrill doesn’t agree with Moody’s that profits are peaking yet — and they say sentiment is bearish enough that, in the normal way of the market, the poor sentiment on stocks is bullish. At sentiment levels like today’s, the usual 12-month return is 19%, Subramanian writes. The real change is much more volatility.
More volatility “doesn’t mean equity losses,” Subramanian says. ”From 1993 to ‘98, the VIX (volatility index) rose ...amidst 22% annualized total returns for the S&P 500. The best place to be when volatility is rising? High quality stocks.”
Maybe, but today’s economic conditions don’t have much in common with 1993, when stocks were confronting the early stages of a very long, very sharp expansion that would feature the invention of the commercial internet — and passage of much more sensible fiscal policy than last year’s budget-busting tax cuts.
Today, as other experts at Merrill point out, we have a maturing housing cycle and mixed signals coming from auto sales month by month. If Vice President Al Gore couldn’t invent the internet, we shouldn’t hold our breath for the next big innovation coming from today’s Mike Pence or, goodness knows, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump.
And while individual tax cuts probably helped consumption in 2018, there’s no new tax cut coming next year to seed new growth. Wage gains after inflation are tiny, too.
And we have the new wild cards of trade tensions — entirely engineered by the administration — and the prospect of a China growth slowdown that may or may not be driven by talk of tariffs.
Trump thinks this is all good — he tweeted Tuesday that tariff wars build respect and will get U.S. companies better access to China’s market at some point (or, if they don’t work, raise taxes on American consumers, which he argues is also good) — but the fact is, a China slowdown will hurt exporters like United Tech, Cat and Deere DE, -2.10% .
Not for nothing did CFRA Research cut its weighting on industrials to underweight from overweight last night, citing “weakening technical trends and escalating uncertainty regarding global trade.”
Growth hiccups in China translate into market hiccups in the U.S., or at least they did in late 2015 and much of 2016, when the S&P fell 12% and even Apple AAPL, -1.49% lost about 30% of its value as sales to Greater China slipped. Trump might know that if his business model had ever been more sophisticated than borrowing money against his inheritance and sometimes paying it back.
For investors a little bit less benighted, the watchword has to be caution. A handful of earnings misses, and a slowdown in guidance growth, isn’t a crisis.
But it’s not a good sign, either. Things look worse than they did even after Netflix’s beat less than two weeks ago. And if tariffs on Chinese goods do spike in 2019, as Trump threatens, the short term is not likely to be pretty.
